items.title: There were ten human Sikh Gurus — the eleventh is the scripture
items.claim: How does the Sikh tradition handle leadership after Guru Gobind Singh?

options.text: It ended after the tenth Guru with no continuation
In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh declared the Guru Granth Sahib (the scripture) to be the eternal Guru — no further human gurus
It continues through a hereditary line

items.reveal:
Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708 from a stab wound inflicted by an Afghan assassin. Before his death he installed the Adi Granth (compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604) as Guru Granth Sahib — making the scripture the eternal Guru.

The Guru Granth Sahib (1,430 pages, mostly in Gurmukhi script) contains hymns by six of the ten Gurus, plus 15 other Hindu and Muslim saints (bhagats) — including Kabir and Sheikh Farid. It is treated as a living Guru: bowed to, awakened in the morning, put to rest at night.

Sikh gurdwaras have the Guru Granth Sahib on a throne (palki) as the central focus.
items.why: The structural innovation of designating scripture as eternal Guru ended succession disputes that plague many religions. Sikh community continuity rests on the text, not on a living hierarchy.

items.title: The Four Noble Truths are the Buddha's core teaching
items.claim: What are the Four Noble Truths?

options.text: Dukkha (suffering exists), Samudaya (its cause is craving/tanha), Nirodha (it can cease), Magga (the path — the Eightfold Path)
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort

items.reveal:
The Buddha is said to have taught the Four Noble Truths in his first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) at Sarnath, near Varanasi, after his enlightenment. They are framed as a medical diagnosis: symptom, cause, prognosis, treatment.

'Dukkha' is often translated 'suffering' but more accurately covers unsatisfactoriness, impermanence, the inability of conditioned things to give lasting peace. 'Tanha' is craving — including for existence and non-existence, not just for pleasure.

The Eightfold Path (the Fourth Noble Truth) is grouped into wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, action, livelihood) and mental discipline (right effort, mindfulness, concentration).
items.why: Buddhism is often summarised as 'life is suffering' — a misleading reduction. The Four Noble Truths are a structured argument from problem to solution, not a pessimistic mood.

items.title: Buddhism has no creator god
items.claim: Does Buddhism teach the existence of a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is the supreme deity worshipped as such
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana Buddhism affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher.
items.why: Western religious frameworks define 'religion' through theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.
